ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Prior to this, ethics clearance was obtained from the ethics board of the University of Groningen, Campus Fryslân.
Since our participants are expecting parents and therefore do not yet need child-directed resources, we use the term 'resources' hereafter to refer to language-related, parent-directed resources.

As pregnancy represents a salient transition into parenthood during which expecting parents likely begin actively considering and preparing for their child's upbringing, including decisions concerning language use, we predicted that most participants had made their language transmission decision during pregnancy (P1).

However, as noted above, all participants were raising their children multilingually: either with the two SLs or with one/both SL(s) and at least one HL. Ahooja et al. (2024) consequently suggested that both participant groups may have relied on largely the same resources, most of which were designed with the two SLs in mind.

(2024)</ref> consequently suggested that both participant groups may have relied on largely the same resources, most of which were designed with the two SLs in mind.

table.text: Participants were recruited via local media, institutional newsletters, social media pages, as well as with posters and flyers placed in locations frequented by parents (e.g. healthcare practitioners, kindergartens, and libraries).
Additionally, snowball sampling was used: participants were asked to share the link to the questionnaire with other parents.
Based on preregistered inclusion criteria, we analysed responses from 520 out of the 642 participants in the original dataset.

Participants were included if they were between 18 and 59 years old, lived in Fryslân, reported at least minimal Frisian proficiency, were raising a young child, and responded to at least 77% of the key items related to the variables in this study.
This is likely related to the fact that the majority of participants had already decided which language(s) to transmit long before they were actually expecting a child (RQ1).
The resources whose influence we examined were thus provided at a point when most participants had already made up their mind regarding the IGT of Frisian.

While the Heit & Mem magazine and, to a lesser extent, the Heit & Mem website are resources for which expecting parents reported high levels of awareness, the available leaflet and booklets were relatively unknown among our participants while they were expecting.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: Since our participants are expecting parents and therefore do not yet need child-directed resources, we use the term 'resources' hereafter to refer to language-related, parent-directed resources.

As pregnancy represents a salient transition into parenthood during which expecting parents likely begin actively considering and preparing for their child's upbringing, including decisions concerning language use, we predicted that most participants had made their language transmission decision during pregnancy (P1).

However, as noted above, all participants were raising their children multilingually: either with the two SLs or with one/both SL(s) and at least one HL. Ahooja et al. (2024) consequently suggested that both participant groups may have relied on largely the same resources, most of which were designed with the two SLs in mind.

Participants were recruited via local media, institutional newsletters, social media pages, as well as with posters and flyers placed in locations frequented by parents (e.g. healthcare practitioners, kindergartens, and libraries).
Additionally, snowball sampling was used: participants were asked to share the link to the questionnaire with other parents.
Based on preregistered inclusion criteria, we analysed responses from 520 out of the 642 participants in the original dataset.

Participants were included if they were between 18 and 59 years old, lived in Fryslân, reported at least minimal Frisian proficiency, were raising a young child, and responded to at least 77% of the key items related to the variables in this study.
This is likely related to the fact that the majority of participants had already decided which language(s) to transmit long before they were actually expecting a child (RQ1).
The resources whose influence we examined were thus provided at a point when most participants had already made up their mind regarding the IGT of Frisian.

While the Heit & Mem magazine and, to a lesser extent, the Heit & Mem website are resources for which expecting parents reported high levels of awareness, the available leaflet and booklets were relatively unknown among our participants while they were expecting.

Europe has long been characterised by a rich linguistic diversity that constitutes an important part of European cultural heritage, yet many of its languages are currently under threat: an estimated 221 of the languages spoken within the European Union are considered to be endangered (UNESCO 2010).
Successful minority language maintenance and revitalisation depend heavily on intergenerational transmission (IGT) within the home (e.g.
De Houwer 2021; Fishman 2001).

text.text: Effective language transmission, in turn, is dependent on the language exposure -and specifically, the quantity and quality of the input -provided to young children by their parents and other caregivers (e.g. Byers-Heinlein et al. 2025).

text.text: Recent research has shown that, to ensure their children receive sufficient minority language exposure, parents often make use of -or at least want to make use of -different types of language-related resources (e.g. Ahooja et al. 2024).

text.text: This includes both parent-directed and child-directed resources: parent-directed resources are leaflets, books, websites, and other materials providing parents with information about raising children multilingually; child-directed resources are storybooks, games, digital applications, and other materials parents can use to engage with their children in the languages they wish to transmit in order to foster their acquisition (Ahooja et al. 2024).

text.text: To date, parental engagement with resources has only been studied with regard to parents who are currently raising a young child.
There is no known research regarding expecting parents' engagement with resources as a way to prepare themselves for the IGT of minority languages.
We argue that this is an important area of empirical inquiry as it seems likely that parents decide on the language(s) they want to transmit prior to the birth of their children.
The timing of (expecting) parents' language transmission decisions, however, has also not yet been investigated.
The aim of our study is to begin filling these gaps in the research literature.

The study examines both the timing of language transmission decisions as well as expecting parents' engagement with language-related resources to foster IGT of minority languages, and we approach these topics within the family language policy (FLP) framework.
FLP is the 'explicit and overt planning in relation to language use within the home among family members' (King et al. 2008: 1).
text.formatted: FLP is the 'explicit and overt planning in relation to language use within the home among family members' <ref type="bibr">(King et al. 2008: 1)</ref>.

text.text: Based on Spolsky's (2004) more general model of language policy, FLP comprises three inter-related components: language beliefs, language practices, and language management (e.g. King et al. 2008).
text.formatted: Based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Spolsky's (2004)</ref> more general model of language policy, FLP comprises three inter-related components: language beliefs, language practices, and language management (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">King et al. 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Language beliefs comprise parents' ideologies (e.g.
Curdt-Christiansen 2009), attitudes (e.g.
Slavkov 2017), and concerns (e.g. Quirk et al. 2026) regarding language(s) and linguistic phenomena such as multilingual child-rearing.

text.text: Language practices are everyday language behaviours within the family: for example, the languages parents choose to speak with their children, how regularly they use them, and the circumstances in which they do so (e.g. Surrain 2021).

text.text: Language management consists of family members' efforts to influence or modify children's language acquisition and use, for instance by adopting specific family language strategies (e.g. Sander-Montant et al. 2025) and/or engaging with language-related resources (Ahooja et al. 2024).

text.text: Systematic research distinguishing between parents' engagement with parent-directed and child-directed resources in minority language contexts outside of Québec is currently lacking.
We are also unaware of any previous research regarding expecting parents' engagement with language-related resources.

However, these studies used different terminology and did not distinguish between parent-directed and child-directed resources.
The present study addresses these gaps by examining expecting parents' engagement with resources in Fryslân, a province in the Netherlands.
Since our participants are expecting parents and therefore do not yet need child-directed resources, we use the term 'resources' hereafter to refer to language-related, parent-directed resources.
The majority language in the Netherlands is Dutch.

Approximately 2% of the country's population also speak West Frisian (Schmeets and Cornips 2026), most of whom live in the province of Fryslân, where they constitute roughly 64% of inhabitants (Dekker et al. 2025).

text.text: Two other closely related Frisian languages are spoken in Germany: North Frisian, with approximately 4,000-5,000 speakers in the district of Nordfriesland (Versloot 2021), and Saterfrisian, the only surviving variety of East Frisian, with an estimated 2,000 speakers in the Saterland municipality (Litty et al. 2026).

text.text: While all three share an ancestor, they are now classified as distinct autochthonous heritage languages (Litty et al. 2026) 1 that are either vulnerable (West Frisian) or severely endangered (North Frisian and East-/Saterfrisian) (UNESCO 2010).

text.text: This study focuses solely on West Frisian, which is hereafter referred to as 'Frisian'.
Almost all Frisian speakers also speak Dutch (e.g.
Hilton et al. 2020), and some know additional languages such as English and/or immigrant HLs.
In recent decades, Frisian has received increasing protection and promotion through language policies and planning measures.
Consequently, the language benefits from greater institutional support, greater visibility in the media and the linguistic landscape, and inclusion in school curricula (see e.g.
Kuipers-Zandberg and Kircher 2020, for an overview of the ethnolinguistic vitality of Frisian).
Furthermore, systematic efforts have been made to encourage the IGT of Frisian in the home.
Nonetheless, the number of parents who transmit Frisian to their children has not increased significantly since the 1970s (e.g. Klinkenberg et al. 2018).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, the number of parents who transmit Frisian to their children has not increased significantly since the 1970s (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Klinkenberg et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To investigate expecting parents' engagement with resources to support them in the IGT of Frisian in Fryslân, we collected quantitative and qualitative questionnaire data from 520 Frisian-speaking parents of young children (aged 0-4 years) who reflected retrospectively on the period during which they were expecting.
Our sample included both parents who ended up transmitting Frisian and parents who did not.
The aim of the study is twofold.
First, we aim to contribute to FLP theory by generating new knowledge regarding language management preparation in the form of expecting parents' engagement with resources.
Second, we aim to provide practical information to policy makers and language planners to help shape future support measures for the IGT of Frisian.
To do so, we investigate the following: first, the timing of minority language speakers' decision as to whether (or not) to transmit Frisian, and second, their engagement with resources.
The latter includes expecting parents' awareness and use of, as well as their desire for, resources.
Finally, we look at whether expecting parents' engagement with these resources has affected their decision (not) to transmit Frisian.
Since this study addresses a previously unexplored stage of FLP, our initial approach was to address our research questions (RQs) in an exploratory fashion.
Therefore, rather than formulating formal hypotheses, we stated predictions (Ps) regarding the patterns we expected to observe.
To contextualise our study, we will first present the prior research that informed our study.
An important first step is to examine when parents decide what language(s) to transmit.
Research on this topic is rare, and has focused primarily on how and why parents made language-related decisions rather than when the decision-making took place.

In the U.S., a small-scale qualitative study on families raising Spanish-English bilinguals showed that FLP decisions were largely shaped by personal experience with the relevant languages and with multilingualism (King and Fogle 2006).
text.formatted: In the U.S., a small-scale qualitative study on families raising Spanish-English bilinguals showed that FLP decisions were largely shaped by personal experience with the relevant languages and with multilingualism <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(King and Fogle 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a small-scale qualitative study in Norway showed that parents' FLP decisions reflected prior experiences with multilingualism, and often also a desire for continuity across the lifespan (Purkarthofer and Steien 2019).
text.formatted: Similarly, a small-scale qualitative study in Norway showed that parents' FLP decisions reflected prior experiences with multilingualism, and often also a desire for continuity across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Purkarthofer and Steien 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, little is known about the point in time at which parents typically decide which languages to transmit.

Understanding decision timing, alongside expecting parents' engagement with resources, can help determine whether additional and/or different resources are needed, and whether awareness-raising regarding existing resources should be increased.

text.text: To our knowledge, no previous research exists regarding when parents decide which language(s) to transmit.
In Fryslân, after registering the birth of their child with the local municipality, parents receive the taalkado (language gift): a gift box of child-directed and parent-directed resources.
Parents who register the birth online receive a digital 'collect card' that they can use to collect the gift at the town hall.
The initiative was introduced in 2008 as the taaltaske (language bag), continued as the taalkado in 2017, and has since been available to families across the province.

Additionally, the Heit & Mem (Dad & Mum) magazine, intended primarily for parents of young children, offers information on (multilingual) childrearing and advice on fostering children's acquisition of Frisian.
text.formatted: Additionally, the Heit & Mem (Dad & Mum) magazine, intended primarily for parents of young children, offers information on (multilingual) childrearing and advice on fostering children's acquisition of Frisian.

text.text: Expecting parents also receive the special edition Lytse Heit & Mem (Little Dad & Mum) as part of the taalkado.

text.text: However, little is known about the support expecting parents need and want -or when they would like to receive it.
It remains to be ascertained whether the available resources reach parents early enough, and whether additional support for expecting parents would be beneficial.
Therefore, our first RQ was: • RQ1: When did parents decide what language(s) to transmit to their child?

As pregnancy represents a salient transition into parenthood during which expecting parents likely begin actively considering and preparing for their child's upbringing, including decisions concerning language use, we predicted that most participants had made their language transmission decision during pregnancy (P1).

Parents' engagement with resources has only been studied systematically in the Canadian province of Québec, where many inhabitants speak HLs alongside one or both of the societal languages (SLs) -that is, the province's majority language, French, and English, which is a minority language in Québec but the majority language in Canada at large. Ballinger et al. (2022) and Ahooja et al. (2024) looked at differences between HL-transmitting parents (who transmitted one/more HLs in addition to one/both of the SLs) and non-HL-transmitting parents (who only transmitted the two SLs) regarding their awareness and use of, satisfaction with, and desire for resources.

(2022)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ahooja et al. (2024)</ref> looked at differences between HL-transmitting parents (who transmitted one/more HLs in addition to one/both of the SLs) and non-HL-transmitting parents (who only transmitted the two SLs) regarding their awareness and use of, satisfaction with, and desire for resources.

text.text: Their findings showed that non-HL-transmitting parents reported higher awareness of resources than HL-transmitting parents (Ahooja et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Their findings showed that non-HL-transmitting parents reported higher awareness of resources than HL-transmitting parents <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ahooja et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, these findings may not be directly transferable to the Frisian context.

The previous studies examined awareness of resources without focusing on specific languages, whereas the present study focuses specifically on resources designed to support the transmission of the autochthonous HL Frisian.
This led to ask: • RQ2: With regard to their awareness of existing resources, were there differences between expecting parents who did and who did not end up transmitting Frisian?

We reasoned that expecting parents who intend to transmit Frisian were more likely to seek out or pay attention to resources relevant to raising children multilingually with Frisian as they prepared for raising their child.
In contrast, such resources may have been perceived as less relevant by expecting parents who do not intend to transmit Frisian.

Consequently, we predicted that awareness of resources differed between the two groups, with expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian ultimately reporting greater awareness than those who ultimately did not transmit it (P2).

Regarding the use of resources, the aforementioned studies in Québec found no significant differences between HL-transmitting and non-HL-transmitting parents (Ahooja et al. 2024; Ballinger et al. 2022).

text.text: However, as noted above, all participants were raising their children multilingually: either with the two SLs or with one/both SL(s) and at least one HL. Ahooja et al. (2024)</ref> consequently suggested that both participant groups may have relied on largely the same resources, most of which were designed with the two SLs in mind.

text.text: At the same time, research elsewhere demonstrated that HL-transmitting parents actively sought information and support related to multilingual child-rearing.

For example, the participants of a small-scale qualitative study in the U.S. reported obtaining information about HL maintenance through newspapers, magazines, schools, teachers, community programmes, paediatricians, and communication with other parents (e.g. Lee et al. 2015).
text.formatted: For example, the participants of a small-scale qualitative study in the U.S. reported obtaining information about HL maintenance through newspapers, magazines, schools, teachers, community programmes, paediatricians, and communication with other parents (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lee et al. 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a small-scale qualitative study in Canada showed that HL-transmitting parents used resources when seeking advice on multilingual childrearing (Barbeau-Morrison 2019).

Given the lack of previous studies regarding expecting parents, it remains unclear whether resource use differs between expecting parents who ultimately transmit a HL to their children and those who do not.
Our third RQ therefore was: • RQ3: With regard to their use of existing resources, were there differences between expecting parents who did and who did not end up transmitting Frisian?
Existing research has compared parents raising their children with different combinations of SLs and HLs, but not parents who do and do not transmit an autochthonous HL.
In the present study, the resources specifically concerned multilingual child-rearing and/or the transmission of Frisian.
We assumed that these resources were more relevant to parents who were considering transmitting Frisian and may therefore have been more likely to seek them out or encounter them.
By contrast, parents who did not (intend to) transmit Frisian may have perceived these resources as less relevant.
We therefore predicted that expecting parents who ultimately did transmit Frisian reported greater resource use than those who ultimately did not transmit Frisian (P3).
As for the satisfaction with resources, the aforementioned Québec-based studies found significant differences between non-HL-transmitting and HL-transmitting parents.

The former reported being satisfied with the available resources, the latter were less satisfied -presumably due to the dearth of available resources aimed at supporting the transmission of immigrant HLs in Québec (Ahooja et al. 2024; Ballinger et al. 2022).
text.formatted: The former reported being satisfied with the available resources, the latter were less satisfied -presumably due to the dearth of available resources aimed at supporting the transmission of immigrant HLs in Québec <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ahooja et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Ballinger et al. 2022</ref>).

text.text: However, it is unclear whether this translates to the Frisian context.
Our fourth RQ was thus: • RQ4: With regard to their satisfaction with existing resources, were there differences between expecting parents who did and who did not end up transmitting Frisian?

We postulated that resources concerning Frisian transmission were particularly relevant to parents who considered/planned to transmit Frisian, and that they were consequently more aware of these resources (see P2).
We therefore expected that the suspected lower awareness of parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisianfoot_2 would result in lower satisfaction with the available resources.

text.text: Hence, our prediction was that expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian would report higher satisfaction with existing resources than expecting parents who did not end up transmitting it (P4).
Next, we turned to parents' desire for additional resources.

Prior research amongst parents raising young children consistently demonstrated their desire for more resources to support their multilingual childrearing practices -and, in the case of HL-transmitting parents, the IGT of these HLs.

For instance, in their small-scale focus group study in Québec's urban centre, Montréal, Ballinger et al. (2022) showed that both HL-transmitting and non-HL-transmitting parents wanted more information on multilingual childrearing (e.g. through various formats such as websites, weekly emails, apps, magazines, and public talks).

(2022)</ref> showed that both HL-transmitting and non-HL-transmitting parents wanted more information on multilingual childrearing (e.g. through various formats such as websites, weekly emails, apps, magazines, and public talks).

text.text: In addition, these parents also valued opportunities to connect with other parents through support groups.
Similarly, Ahooja et al. (2024) found that parents throughout Québec expressed a desire for more such resources.

text.text: Other small-scale qualitative studies in the U.S. showed a comparable desire for more affordable and accessible materials supporting HL-transmission (e.g. Kwon 2017).

text.text: This led us to ask: • RQ5: With regard to their desire for additional resources, were there differences between expecting parents who did and who did not end up transmitting Frisian?

We expected that parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian perceived the available resources as less relevant for their language transmission decision (see P1), leading them to desire alternative resources that would better support their language transmission practices.
In contrast, parents who ultimately transmitted Frisian may have perceived existing resources as more relevant to their language practices and therefore felt less of a need for additional resources.

Based on this, we predicted that expecting parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian retrospectively expressed a stronger desire for additional resources than expecting parents who ultimately transmitted Frisian (P5).
Finally, we turn to the relevance of resources to expecting parents' language transmission decisions.
Specifically, we asked: • RQ6: Was the decision to transmit Frisian affected by the available resources?

Resources providing information and support regarding multilingual child-rearing and Frisian transmission may have contributed to parents' decision-making by informing them about the potential benefits, practicalities, and solutions to challenges regarding the IGT of Frisian.
We therefore predicted that the resources they encountered played at least some role in the expecting parents' language transmission decision (P6).

text.text: Participants were recruited via local media, institutional newsletters, social media pages, as well as with posters and flyers placed in locations frequented by parents (e.g. healthcare practitioners, kindergartens, and libraries).
Additionally, snowball sampling was used: participants were asked to share the link to the questionnaire with other parents.
Data were collected between February and June 2025.
Prior to this, ethics clearance was obtained from the ethics board of the University of Groningen, Campus Fryslân.
Based on preregistered inclusion criteria, we analysed responses from 520 out of the 642 participants in the original dataset.

Participants were included if they were between 18 and 59 years old, lived in Fryslân, reported at least minimal Frisian proficiency, were raising a young child, and responded to at least 77% of the key items related to the variables in this study.
The final sample comprised parents from all regions in Fryslân except for the islands of Schiermonnikoog and Vlieland.
The mean Frisian proficiency for understanding was 3.94 (SD=0.18) and speaking 3.69 (SD=0.65), measured on Likert scales where 0 meant not proficient at all and 4 meant highly proficient.
Most participants spoke Frisian as their sole L1 (63.85%) or as one of their L1s alongside Dutch (23.65%).
Most were raising their child with a partner (96.15%), identified as female (85,58%), and had chosen to transmit Frisian either as the sole language (44.61%) or alongside Dutch (49.23%).
Out of the Frisian-transmitting parents, 92.12% of respondents indicated speaking Frisian to their child themselves and 77.50% indicated the co-caregiver transmitted Frisian.
Participants' children were fairly balanced, and their ages are depicted in Figure 1.

text.text: The timing of participants' language transmission decision was elicited through a multiple-choice question (Q19) asking when they had decided which language(s) to raise their child with.

Response options were "more than three months before the pregnancy", "three months or less before the pregnancy", "during the pregnancy", "within the first three months after my child's birth", "later than the first three months after my child's birth", and "I am unsure".
Participants' awareness and use of resources were measured via multiple-select questions (Q49 and Q50, respectively).

Response options were the materials included in the taalkado: the Talen kleuren je leven (Languages colour your life) leaflet, the Yn ferwachting (Expecting) booklet, and the Hoera in lytse poppe (Hurrah a little baby) booklet.
The two other main resources that are available, namely the Heit & Mem magazine and the Heit & mem website, were also included.
text.formatted: The two other main resources that are available, namely the Heit & Mem magazine and the Heit & mem website, were also included.

text.text: Additional answer options allowed participants to indicate that they were unaware of these resources (Q49) or had not used any of them before their child's birth (Q50).
For Q50, participants could also indicate that they had used other resources, prompting an open-ended follow-up question to elicit details.
Satisfaction with existing resources was measured via a five-point Likert item (Q51), ranging from "not satisfied at all" to "very satisfied".

Participants' desire for additional resources was measured with a multiple-choice item (Q53), asking whether they would have liked additional resources while expecting their child, with the answer options "yes", "no", and "I am not sure".
The selection of "yes" prompted another open-ended follow-up question, asking participants to elaborate on the additional resources they would have liked to receive prior to their child's birth.
Finally, the effect of resources on transmission was measured via a fivepoint Likert item (Q52), ranging from "not at all" to "completely".
Several methods were used to address our research questions.
RQ1 (decision timing) and RQ6 (effect of resources) were addressed using descriptive statistics: namely numbers and percentages.
For awareness (RQ2), use (RQ3), satisfaction (RQ4), and desire (RQ5), we first computed average scores.
For awareness (RQ2) and use (RQ3), these were the total number of resources participants selected in response to each question.
The average satisfaction score (RQ4) was the overall satisfaction measured on the 5-point Likert item in Q51.
Linear regression was then used to answer RQ2, RQ3, and RQ4, with the relevant average score as the dependent variable and language transmission decision as the independent variable.
Participants with missing variables for the separate regression analyses were excluded for these analyses.
In cases where strong deviations from normality and/or homogeneity of variance were observed, robustness checks using non-parametric alternatives (e.g.
Wilcoxon rank sum tests) were additionally used to verify the stability of findings.

text.text: Responses containing multiple distinct desired resources were coded separately and therefore led to multiple codes per unit.
Coding was inductive and data-driven, with codes remaining as close as possible to participants' wording while capturing the underlying type of support requested.

Analyses followed three main stages: (1) familiarisation with the dataset and generation of initial descriptive codes; (2) comparison of initial codes across the complete dataset, grouping into broader conceptual categories, development of a coding manual with definitions, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, and examples; and (3) application of the coding manual to the full dataset and possible revisions to the coding manual.

text.text: In line with P1, our findings indicate that the decision to transmit Frisian was generally made before the birth of the child.

However, this decision was made even earlier than we had assumed, namely well in advance of pregnancy, with more than three quarters of participants reporting that the decision had been made more than three months before pregnancy.
A small group of participants made the decision during pregnancy, and only very few reported deciding after their child was born (see Table 1).

In line with P3, participants who ended up transmitting Frisian reported using significantly more resources than those that did not (mean=0.94, sd=0.97, and mean=0.44, sd=0.72, respectively; β=0.498, SE=0.175, t(512)=2.846, p=.00461).
The model explained a small proportion of the variance in use (R²=.016, adjusted R²=.014).
A Wilcoxon rank-sum test, used as a robustness check for non-parametric data, indicated the same increased use by participants who ended up transmitting Frisian (W=5,432, p=.002865).

Most expecting parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian reported using none of the listed resources, with a large group of expecting parents who ultimately did transmit Frisian reporting the same.

Contrary to P4, there was no significant difference in the satisfaction with available resources between expecting participants who ended up transmitting Frisian and those who did not (mean=3.33, sd=1.26, and mean=2.96, sd=1.23, respectively).

Both the regression analysis (β=0.365, SE=0.2447, t(470)=1.49, p=.137) and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test used as a robustness check for non-parametric data (W=5,023, p=.07739) indicated no statistically significant difference between the two groups.

It is worth noting, however, that this question was answered by almost all expecting parents that did not end up transmitting Frisian (n=28) and the majority of this group (n=22) had previously indicated that they had not actually used any of the previously listed resources.

Although descriptive statistics indicated a greater desire for additional resources among participants who ended up transmitting Frisian than among those that did not (12.73% "yes" versus 0.00% "yes", respectively), and fewer "not sure" responses (27.10% versus 34.38%, respectively), these differences did not reach statistical significance (p=.060).
The results therefore do not support P5 as there is insufficient evidence of transmission decisions being associated with participants' desire for additional resources.

text.text: This study aimed to contribute to FLP theory by generating knowledge regarding expecting parents' engagement with resources as a form of language management preparation, as well as providing practical information to policy makers and language planners to help shape future support measures for the IGT of Frisian in Fryslân.
As this is the first ever study of any aspect of FLP among expecting parents, our findings cannot be compared with research from other contexts.
Accordingly, the discussion focuses on the findings of the current study and provides general recommendations.
We predicted that during the pregnancy would be the most commonly reported time during which minority language speakers decide whether (or not) to transmit Frisian (P1).
Yet, our findings showed that this decision was often made even earlier: namely, in most cases, well before pregnancy.

A parallel project investigating the IGT of Frisian in Nordfriesland revealed a similar pattern: the vast majority of minority language speakers had made the decision well before pregnancy, while considerably fewer made the decision during the pregnancy, and only a handful decided during the first few months of the child's life (Kircher and Heinzova, in preparation).
text.formatted: A parallel project investigating the IGT of Frisian in Nordfriesland revealed a similar pattern: the vast majority of minority language speakers had made the decision well before pregnancy, while considerably fewer made the decision during the pregnancy, and only a handful decided during the first few months of the child's life <ref type="bibr">(Kircher and Heinzova, in preparation)</ref>.

text.text: The early timing of minority language speakers' language transmission decision suggests that, if they are to be helpful for individuals who are planning to have a family, relevant resources ought to be available well before pregnancy, rather than being introduced only during pregnancy or after birth (as is currently the case with the aforementioned taalkado).

Moreover, the finding that Frisian speakers typically decide which language(s) to transmit more than three months prior to pregnancy points to the need to consider this early family planning stage as an important phase in the development of FLP.
We predicted that expecting parents who ultimately ended up transmitting Frisian would report greater awareness of existing resources (P2).
This was supported by our findings: expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian reported significantly greater awareness of resources than those who did not transmit the language.
The Heit & Mem magazine was identified as the most well-known resource.
text.formatted: The Heit & Mem magazine was identified as the most well-known resource.

text.text: The other resources, namely the leaflet and booklets included in the taalkado, were much less known by both groups of expecting parents.

One possible explanation for this is that we asked parents about their retrospective awareness of the specific materials contained in the taalkado instead of asking whether they were aware of the taalkado itself.
It is possible that parents were aware of the existence of a taalkado without being aware of the exact contents.
Future research is necessary to find out about this.
We predicted that expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian would report using significantly more resources than expecting parents who did not end up transmitting Frisian (P3).
The findings supported our prediction.

As the resources mentioned in the questionnaire specifically concerned raising children multilingually with Frisian, expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian likely used them for their intended purpose.
By contrast, expecting parents who did not end up transmitting Frisian likely had less need for resources to support a language transmission decision they did not make.
Out of all identified resources, the Heit & Mem magazine was the most frequently used among both groups of expecting parents.
text.formatted: Out of all identified resources, the Heit & Mem magazine was the most frequently used among both groups of expecting parents.

text.text: This is in line with the fact that it was the resource that the most expecting parents from both groups were aware of.
The Heit & Mem website was also used relatively frequently by expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian.
text.formatted: The Heit & Mem website was also used relatively frequently by expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian.

text.text: Both groups of expecting parents reported little use of the Talen kleuren je leven leaflet and the Yn ferwachting and Hoera in lytse poppe booklets.

A possible explanation for this is that these materials arrived too late in the family language planning process, as the vast majority of participants indicated that -by the time they were expecting a child -they had already decided on whether (or not) to transfer Frisian.
Again, more research is needed to ascertain this.
We predicted that there would be a difference in satisfaction with existing resources between expecting parents who ended up transmitting Frisian and those who did not (P4).
However, the findings did not support this: satisfaction with available resources did not differ significantly between the two groups.
A possible explanation for this is the retrospective nature of the questionnaire.
Participants may have evaluated their satisfaction with available resources based on their current circumstances rather than their experiences at the time they actually were expecting their child.

We suspect this because, while the majority of the expecting parents that did not end up transmitting Frisian had indicated that they had used none of the aforementioned resources (see Figure 3), they did indicate being satisfied with the materials that they had used.

text.text: Our findings do not support P5: there was no statistically significant association between Frisian transmission and expecting parents' desire for additional resources.

Expecting parents who ended up not transmitting Frisian indicated no desire for additional resources, and only a small share of expecting parents who did end up transmitting Frisian indicated a desire for additional resources.
Specifically, they would have liked to receive information on bilingual child-rearing, (earlier) access to the resources mentioned in the questionnaire, and child-directed entertainment materials.

Some participants noted that they did not receive a taalkado because their child was born in hospital outside of Fryslân,foot_5 and they consequently had to register the child's birth in a different province.

text.text: This made them ineligible to receive a taalkado.

This is also related to the awareness of the taalkado: participants who expressed a desire for (earlier) access to the taalkado often indicated that, at the time, they did not know it existed, and that they would have liked to have received it.

Although the need for additional resources exists, it is possible that we failed to find significant differences between the expecting parent groups simply due to the small sample size of the parents who did not end up transmitting Frisian.
Future research could clarify whether this is the case.
Finally, the results revealed that, for most expecting parents, the available resources did not play a significant role in their decision of whether (or not) to transmit Frisian.
These findings therefore do not support P6.
More than half of the participants indicated that the question did not apply, while a fifth reported no influence at all.
This is likely related to the fact that the majority of participants had already decided which language(s) to transmit long before they were actually expecting a child (RQ1).
The resources whose influence we examined were thus provided at a point when most participants had already made up their mind regarding the IGT of Frisian.

Still, there were some participants who indicated making the decision during pregnancy; and for minority language speakers like them, the qualitative data indicated a need for the resources that are currently offered post-birth to be provided sooner, to support the decision-making process of at least that share of expecting parents.
There is a possibility that the resources, if provided earlier in the FLP process, could affect parents' language transmission decision.
The present study was the first to examine expecting parents' engagement with resources as a form of language management preparation.
Due to the non-representative nature of the participant sample, we make no claims about the generalisation of our findings.

Nonetheless, the findings provide meaningful insights that -if they do generalise -have important implications for language policy and planning to promote the IGT of Frisian in Fryslân, and thereby the minority language's maintenance and revitalisation.

Notably, our finding that Frisian speakers tend to decide which language(s) to transfer to their children more than three months prior to pregnancy indicates that relevant resources aiming to foster the IGT of Frisian in Fryslân should be made available much earlier than is currently the case.

Providing such resources to Frisian speakers who are in the early phases of family planning, before they are even expecting a child, ought to help them make informed language transmission decisions during the stage at which they actually tend to consider which language(s) to transmit.
Additionally, our results reveal the importance of increasing awareness of existing resources for expecting parents.

While the Heit & Mem magazine and, to a lesser extent, the Heit & Mem website are resources for which expecting parents reported high levels of awareness, the available leaflet and booklets were relatively unknown among our participants while they were expecting.

text.text: It is therefore advisable to design measures that raise awareness of the resources that are currently available for expecting parents as well as any resources that are developed in the future for Frisian speakers in the early stages of the family planning process.
Raising awareness of these resources could support anyone who is unsure about whether to transmit Frisian.
Some parents retrospectively reflected on not having received the taalkado as they gave birth in hospital outside of Fryslân and consequently were ineligible for the taalkado.
To counter this, we suggest making the taalkado available based on the family's place of residence rather than the child's place of birth.
If there is a desire for the taalkado, it should ideally also be accessible to Frisian-speaking parents outside of Fryslân.

Making these resources not only more visible but also more accessible at an earlier stage could also enhance awareness and use, thereby ensuring that expecting parents receive relevant information when they need it.

In addition to the aforementioned recommendations, we also recommend the organisation of regular public engagement activities on language science that are specifically aimed at expecting parents and parents raising young children.
A holistic approach to language revitalisation should address both parents' knowledge and children's experiences with the target language.

It has been shown that public engagement activities on language science, such as the Kletskoppen (Chatheads) festival, increase primary school-aged children's positive attitudes towards multilingualism (Unsworth and Knopp 2026).

text.text: Implementing similar activities and meetings specifically for expecting parents and parents raising young children in Fryslân could bring families together, foster the creation of support networks, provide opportunities for positive interactions with and in Frisian, and contribute to the dissemination of evidencebased information about minority language transmission and multilingual child-rearing.
Such events would also constitute an excellent venue for introducing (expecting) parents to existing resources and highlighting when and how these resources can be accessed.
These recommendations, alongside recommendations based on the aforementioned other components of our project, are currently being written up in a comprehensive research report.

The aim of this research-informed science communication is to provide policy makers and language planners with the knowledge that is necessary to create effective support measures for families in Fryslân who wish to raise their children (multilingually) with Frisian.
Previous research has shown that such support measures are most likely to be effective if they are tailored to families' specific situations (Fibla et al. 2022).

text.text: There are three major ways in which our study differs from previously-published research regarding resources.
First, our study focuses on expecting parents' engagement with resources -so, prior to the birth of their children.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine expecting parents' awareness and use of, satisfaction with, and desire for resources of any kind and in any context.

Second, while the aforementioned studies focused on parents who were raising their children multilingually with different language constellations, the current study is the first to compare parents who ended up raising their child multilingually or monolingually, with or without their HL.
Third, our study is set in a previously unexplored context: namely the province of Fryslân in the Netherlands.

As the resources investigated in our study are specific to Frisian in Fryslân, and our sample was sizable but not representative, we make no claims regarding the generalisation of the study's findings to other minority language contexts.
Especially the comparatively smaller sub-sample of expecting parents who did not end up transmitting Frisian does not allow for this.

Despite repeated efforts to reach parents who were part of this target group, and even an extension of the time period during which our data were collected, we did not reach the sub-sample size we had aimed for during the preregistration.

A potential explanation for this lies in the topic of the questionnaire: (expecting) parents who did not end up transmitting Frisian could have had less interest in participating in research on the transmission of Frisian, or they could have felt ashamed about their decision not to pass Frisian on to their child.

Follow-up interviews with participants who did not end up transmitting Frisian, but who indicated a willingness to participate in further research, could help clarify the reasons, and such follow-up interviews could also reveal other ways to reach and recruit this target group.

Retrospectively looking at parents' engagement with resources during the time they were expecting a child constituted a very useful first step towards gaining insights into the FLP dynamics of expecting parents, and specifically their language management preparation.
Ideally, future research should also examine data collected from minority language speakers at the time they were actually expecting a child.
This will yield additional insights regarding their awareness and use of, satisfaction with, and desire for resources.

Since there are no known studies of expecting parents in other contexts, future research could ascertain which of our findings are Fryslân-specific and which findings characterise expecting parents' language management preparation across contexts.
